In the middle and later nineteenth century European musicians took a strong interest in this exotic instrument and began to improve and adapt it. In the Victorian era the nose flute became a popular instrument of home entertainment, and dedicated tutors and music for it even appeared. The modern nose flute has become a ceramic or plastic product, a representative folk instrument around the world that keeps its distinctive cultural heritage.

Occasions of playing include courtship and private playing in Hawaii, where the flute may accompany chanting, song and hula; in Taiwan the double-pipe Paiwan nose flute is used at weddings and funerals, in sacrifice, to welcome guests and to pass on messages; Chuukese men once played traditional love songs on the nose flute; and the Maori formerly had flute playing accompany hymns while tattooing.

Bamboo is common in Hawaii, the Philippines, Micronesia, Fiji, Tonga and among the indigenous peoples of Taiwan; in Hawaii it is a single joint of bamboo, and Micronesia may use bamboo or mangrove root. The Maori nguru of New Zealand is carved from wood, gourd stem and whale tooth, while the kōauau ponga ihu is a gourd; modern metal nose flutes are of metal. This distinctive instrument played an important part in the daily life and rituals of the islanders of old, being used in religious sacrifice, social gatherings and entertainment. Nose flutes are usually made of bamboo, bone or shell, and rely on resonance in the nasal cavity to produce a warm, gentle timbre.

The nose flute is an aerophone, classification number 421.111.22, sounded by blowing through the nasal cavity; most have a mouthpiece and fingerholes, and some set the pitch by controlling the speed of the air or by changing the volume of the mouth. They are found in Polynesia, around the Pacific rim, in Africa, Southeast Asia and Europe, and the various versions need not be historically related — they are grouped together because the way of playing is similar. Players include Hawaiians, eight peoples of the Congo, Tanzanians, the Bontoc and Kalinga of the Philippines, the Paiwan and Rukai of Taiwan, the Chuukese of Micronesia, the Maori of New Zealand and the peoples of Fiji and Tonga, on occasions such as courtship, weddings and funerals, sacrifice, welcoming guests, passing on messages and traditional love songs.
